# Ezekiel 13: Verse-by-Verse Research Notes

**What I found, in brief:** The commentators I read agree on what the chapter means. I didn't find any verse where Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed or Lutheran teachers clearly disagree. The real disagreements are between individual commentators on a few verses (v. 9, v. 10, v. 18), not between church traditions. I've marked a tradition only where the site itself labels the writer.

**What I couldn't find (I ran out of searches):** Orthodox sources (oca.org), modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, NET Bible notes), Lutheran, Pentecostal or Wesleyan sources that deal with this chapter, and anything on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching. Most of those sections are missing below for that reason. Guzik's Enduring Word page was also cut off partway through v. 18, so I have nothing from him on vv. 19–21.

---

## Part 1: The traditional reading

**Background to the chapter**
- Constable says chapter 13 follows naturally from chapter 12. There God corrected his people's wrong ideas; here he rebukes the people responsible for them. The chapter deals with two groups: male false prophets (vv. 1–16) and female false prophets (vv. 17–23). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-13.html
- The Pulpit Commentary links the chapter to Ezekiel 12:21–28 and Jeremiah 23. It notes there were false prophets and prophetesses among the exiles as well as in Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/13.htm

**v. 1–2**
- Guzik says these false prophets mostly gave an upbeat message: God would rescue Jerusalem, and the exiles would soon come home. Following Block, he thinks the repeated phrase "prophets of Israel who prophesy" is sarcastic. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-13/
- Guzik also says the source of "their own heart" (BSB "their own imagination") wasn't necessarily demonic. Their own wishes, wisdom and need for approval shaped what they said. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-13/
- Constable says "prophet" is used ironically here. He quotes Stuart, who compares pretending to be a prophet to impersonating a police officer. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-13.html
- Haydock (Catholic) says "heart" means whatever pleased them, without inspiration. Such frauds always existed, and they did great harm to ignorant people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-13.html

**v. 3**
- The Pulpit Commentary notes a pun in the Hebrew: the *nabiim* (prophets) are also the *n'balim* (fools). Their sin was following their own spirit instead of the Spirit of the LORD. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/13.htm
- Ligonier connects "foolish" to Psalm 14:1, where the fool denies God. So Ezekiel judges these men to have no real relationship with the Lord. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ezekiel-condemns-false-prophets
- Constable says the Hebrew *nabal* describes someone who ignores God's word and relies on himself. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-13.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik thinks the animals are probably jackals rather than foxes, and the setting ruins rather than deserts. The picture is of animals burrowing in rubble and adding nothing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-13/
- Ellicott (labelled Anglican on StudyLight) gives two readings. The simile may simply mean the prophets lived carelessly among their nation's ruins. Or, as many take it, foxes undermining the ground show the prophets speeding up the ruin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/13-4.html
- The Pulpit Commentary lists several points of comparison: cunning (Luke 13:32), spoiling vines (Song 2:15), and burrowing among ruins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/13.htm
- Gill points out it says "thy prophets," not the Lord's. They belonged to Israel because Israel welcomed them, not because God sent them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/13-4.htm

**v. 5**
- The Pulpit Commentary sees two pictures: breaches in Jerusalem's walls (literal and spiritual) and the broken hedge of Israel's vineyard (Isaiah 5:5). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/13.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the breach is the one the nation's sin made. The people who urge repentance are the ones who repair it. They take the "hedge" to be God's law. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Eze/Eze_013.cfm
- Guzik, quoting Alexander, says the prophets lacked courage. They didn't rush to the gaps like brave soldiers. Following Taylor, he identifies "the day of the LORD" here with the fall of Jerusalem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-13/

**v. 6–7**
- The Pulpit Commentary prefers the reading "they hope to confirm their word." Having fooled others, they fooled themselves and really expected their predictions to come true. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/13.htm
- Constable says verse 7 asks them whether their claimed revelations were really just false visions. He quotes Alexander, who applies this to false prophets in religious settings today. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-13.html

**v. 8**
- Guzik notes the reversal: prophets, of all people, should have God on their side, yet he says he is against them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-13/
- Ligonier thinks verses 8–16 probably have in mind the lying prophets who falsely reassured King Zedekiah just before Jerusalem fell in 586 BC. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ezekiel-condemns-false-prophets

**v. 9**
- Keil and Delitzsch see three punishments, each worse than the last: they lose their influence in the council, they are left off the register of citizens of God's kingdom, and they never share in the return to the land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/13-9.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says "council" means a small group of advisers, not a crowd. It reads the register as both an earthly list of citizens and a heavenly register, with the stress on the earthly one. Ezra 2:62 shows such lists being used after the exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/13.htm
- Constable says this means losing citizenship. He cross-references Luke 10:20 and Revelation 3:5. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-13.html

**v. 10**
- The Pulpit Commentary calls "Peace, when there was no peace" the root evil of false prophecy: it lulled consciences to sleep. The "wall" may be some human scheme for safety, such as an alliance with Egypt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/13.htm
- Guzik, quoting Feinberg, says the "untempered mortar" was really whitewash, which does nothing to strengthen a weak wall. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-13/
- Clarke says a true prophet is a wall of defence for the people. He describes how one false prophet makes a claim and another confirms it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/13-10.html
- Ligonier says the prophets ignored the people's sin and covered over the weak nation it had built. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ezekiel-condemns-false-prophets

**v. 11**
- The Pulpit Commentary describes the image as an Eastern storm and links it to Jesus' parable of the two builders (Matthew 7:25). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/13.htm
- Gill identifies the "overflowing shower" as the Babylonian army. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/13-11.htm

**v. 12**
- Ellicott says that once the coming judgments destroyed the basis of their prophecies, everyone would see how foolish and false their words were. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/13-12.htm
- Constable quotes Block: a good outward appearance is no substitute for real soundness. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-13.html

**v. 13–14**
- Constable says the foundations of the people's homes, and of the false prophets' picture of the future, would be laid bare, and the prophets would die in the judgment. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-13.html
- Guzik notes that a falling wall takes lives with it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-13/

**v. 15–16**
- Guzik quotes Wiersbe: the fake prophets gave the people false hope, so God gave them no hope at all. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-13/
- Constable quotes Taylor, who applies this to preachers who like to say pleasing things. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-13.html
- D. A. Carson (The Gospel Coalition) puts the test this way: do teachers call people to repentance, or just paper over the cracks? https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/part-5-when-god-deceives-the-prophets-ezekiel-13-14/

**v. 17**
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that Israel had godly women prophets (Miriam, Deborah, Huldah), so it is natural that there were women on the other side too. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/13.htm
- Guzik, quoting Block, notes that Ezekiel won't give these women the title "prophetess." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-13/
- Constable says God occasionally raised up women prophets, but there was no formal order of them. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-13.html

**v. 18**
- The Pulpit Commentary admits the words are rare and their meaning has to be guessed. The bands may have been amulets. The veils may have been placed over the people who came to consult the women, as a kind of net. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/13.htm
- Constable quotes Cooper: these women were more like witches than prophets. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-13.html
- The Geneva Bible notes describe superstitious women telling fortunes for money. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/13-18.htm

**v. 19**
- Constable quotes Dyer: in some cultures barley was used in the occult, either as an offering to spirits or to try to tell the future. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-13.html
- A homiletical commentary on Bible Hub says they hunted souls through dishonest, unjust oracles. https://biblehub.com/sermons/ezekiel/13-18.htm

**v. 20–21**
- Constable says God would tear off their magic bands and veils and free the people they had trapped like birds. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-13.html
- Matthew Henry says their frauds would be exposed and God's people would no longer be hunted. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/13-18.html

**v. 22**
- Calvin says "the righteous" are the people the false prophets frightened for no reason. This verse explains the "killing" of souls in v. 19. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/13-22.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the righteous were saddened by false predictions of disaster coming on the godly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/13-22.htm

**v. 23**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say events would prove their lies wrong and bring them to ruin. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Eze/Eze_013.cfm
- Constable quotes Stuart, who compares the women to modern fortune tellers. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-13.html

---

## Part 2: Where interpreters disagree

These are differences between commentators, not between denominations.

**v. 9: what is the "register"?**
- **A heavenly book of life:** The Geneva Bible notes take it as the book of life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/13-9.htm Gill adds this, alongside the list of returning exiles, citing the Targum's "writing of eternal life." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/13-9.htm
- **An earthly list:** Calvin says it was a list of people chosen for office, and the frauds were outside the Church. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/13-9.html Ellicott takes it as the family registers of Israel. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/13-9.htm

**v. 10: literal or figurative wall?**
- Constable sets out two readings. In the literal one, the prophets were praising people's actual building projects. In the figurative one, which most commentators hold and he prefers, the "wall" is their false picture of the future. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-13.html
- Utley (bible.org) suggests the false prophets may have been relying on Isaiah's promise that Jerusalem wouldn't fall. But the covenant promises depended on obedience. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-13

**v. 18: what were the "pillows"?**
- Calvin thinks they were placed under the arms of the people consulting the women. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom23/calcom23.ii.xviii.html
- Gill reads them as a sign of ease and false security. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/13-18.htm
- Clarke reports Calmet's view that the word means hunting nets. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/13-18.html

---

## Part 3: Other views

**Catholic**
- **v. 9:** Haydock says they would no longer be consulted or trusted. He also reports a view that their writings would not be counted as Scripture. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-13.html
